report.headline: A textbook example of strong traditional engineering discipline running well ahead of AI-native practice: CI/CD, testing, and review gates are near-exemplary, but there is no agent guidance, no AI process harness, and no agentic review/fix loop anywhere in the repo.
strengths: Comprehensive, gated CI/CD: 7 workflows enforcing lint/test/build, required status checks, and fully automated release-please versioning and deploy
Deep testing culture: 68 test files, 0.76 test-to-source ratio, and sampled unit tests with genuine table-driven behavioral assertions
Disciplined review process: 100% reviewed merges, 93% small-batch PRs, 0% reverted, backed by CODEOWNERS and branch protection
Unusually rigorous internal architecture documentation (docs/architecture/*) with diagrams and traceable metadata that is inherently agent-legible, even though not labeled as such
Solid dependency and pinning hygiene: automated updates plus 26/27 Actions/images pinned by SHA/digest
risks: No CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md or any machine-readable agent guidance exists, so any AI coding agent starts every session with zero repo-specific context
No AI-specific process harness (evals, prompt library, agent runbooks) exists to verify AI-proposed changes before they ship
No AI code-review or auto-fix bot is in the loop — automation is limited to dependency/release bots, not generative-AI assistance
Supply-chain verification has gaps: no SAST, no signed/provenance releases, no SBOM, and 4 of 7 workflows hold broad write permissions

The apparent '83% AI/bot commits' figure is mostly dependency/release-bot noise; only 8% of PRs show real AI involvement, so AI-assisted coding is still a minority, individual practice rather than a systemic one

roadmap.title: There's no harness to verify AI-authored changes before they ship
roadmap.rationale: Branch protection governs human review well, but there's no evals/golden-test layer or agent-facing runbook that would let the team extend trust to AI-driven changes with confidence. Without this, AI usage stays ad hoc and individual rather than something the team can rely on systemically.
explore: What would 'good enough to merge' look like for a change an AI agent proposed here?
Could the existing 68 test files double as a golden-set an agent runs against before proposing a change?
Who on the team would want to define the review gate for AI-assisted or semi-autonomous PRs?

roadmap.title: Dependency automation is mature, but none of the review/fix loop is AI-driven yet
roadmap.rationale: Renovate and the release bot handle version bumps and releases reliably, but there's no AI review bot or LLM-in-CI step — first-pass code review still rests entirely on human reviewers even for low-risk, repetitive changes.
explore: Where does PR review currently spend the most human time that an AI first-pass might usefully absorb?
Would an AI reviewer sit naturally alongside the existing CODEOWNERS/approval gate, or would it compete with it?
Is there appetite to pilot AI review on the lowest-risk PRs — like dependency bumps — before touching anything else?

roadmap.title: Supply-chain trust stops at branch protection — signing, SAST, and SBOM aren't there yet
roadmap.rationale: Pinned dependencies and branch protection are strong, but without SAST, artifact signing/provenance, or SBOM generation — and with 4 of 7 workflows holding broad write tokens — there's a ceiling on how much autonomy could safely be extended to agents that touch CI or release pipelines.
explore: What's currently blocking a CodeQL or Semgrep pass from being added alongside the existing lint/test workflow?
Would signing release artifacts (cosign/SLSA) change how much the team trusts the automated release pipeline?
Do all 4 broad-write workflows genuinely need write access, or could scopes be narrowed per job?

roadmap.title: Most of the 'AI-attributed' commit activity is dependency/release bots, not generative AI coding
roadmap.rationale: The 83% bot-commit figure could create a misleading impression of AI-native maturity when it's largely Renovate and release-please. Only 8% of PRs show direct AI coding involvement — worth the team seeing clearly so effort goes where the real adoption gap is.
explore: When engineers do use Copilot/Claude/etc. day-to-day, does that usage show up in commit trailers, or does it go unrecorded?
Would consistently tagging AI-assisted commits help the team see its own real adoption curve rather than relying on bot noise?

roadmap.title: Agent guidance is thin — coding agents have little to go on when they land in this repo
roadmap.rationale: Without a CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md, every agent session has to rediscover build/test commands, architecture, and constraints from scratch — even though the docs/architecture/ set already contains much of that knowledge in a structured, traceable form. Closing this gap is usually the cheapest lever for making AI contributions safer and faster.
explore: What would it take to point an agent at the existing docs/architecture set as its primary map rather than starting cold?
Which build/test/lint commands do engineers repeat most often when onboarding a new person — would those be worth writing down once for an agent too?
Are there 'never/always' constraints (proto generation, secret handling, k6 runner quirks) that the team already knows by heart but has never had to write down?

discrepancies.claim: The D2 sub-signal claims sampled tests have '0 substantive assertions,' but the four sampled test files (flags_test.go, http_test.go, secret_test.go, db_test.go) each contain multiple require.Equal/NoError/Len calls verifying real behavior (state transitions, JSON redaction, CRUD lifecycle) — this sub-signal appears to be a detector miss.

D5 reports the README has '0 sections,' but the README sample shows clear Setext-style headers ('Probes\n------', 'Run your own private probe\n---------------------') — the section-detection likely only looks for ATX '##' markup and missed the underline-style headings actually present.

report.headline: Tanka is a rigorously engineered, well-governed Go project — excellent CI/CD, review discipline, and a real test suite — but it has essentially no AI-native layer yet: no agent guidance, no agentic workflows in CI, and no AI verification harness exist, so its strong guardrails aren't yet being used to accelerate AI-assisted development.
strengths: A gated, mature delivery pipeline: 7 CI workflows, required status checks, and an automated conventional-commit release process
Strong review culture — 100% of merged PRs reviewed, 95% small-batch PRs, 0% reverted, fast 1.3h median time-to-first-review
Solid security fundamentals: branch protection with signed commits, fully pinned dependencies, active SECURITY.md, automated dependency updates
A real, behaviorally-meaningful test base — 64 test files at a 0.64 test-to-source ratio, including end-to-end acceptance tests against the compiled binary
Living documentation: a dedicated docs site (tanka.dev), auto-generated changelog, and at least one ADR-style design document
risks: No machine-readable agent guidance anywhere in the repo, so any AI-assisted contribution starts from zero context on domain-specific build/test/architecture knowledge

No AI-in-the-loop automation exists (review bots, LLM CI steps, auto-fix loops); the visible 83% bot-commit rate is almost entirely Renovate dependency bumps, not generative-AI-assisted development (only 3% of PRs show AI involvement)

Supply-chain trust has real gaps alongside its strengths: no SAST, no signed/provenance releases, no SBOM, and most workflows don't scope least-privilege permissions — any future autonomous-agent PR pipeline would inherit that broad blast radius
No dedicated AI process harness (evals, prompt libraries, agent runbooks) exists, so there is no repeatable way to verify AI-authored changes before human review
Some tests lean on 'did it error' rather than asserting on specific output/behavior, leaving room for silent regressions to slip past the suite

roadmap.title: Agent guidance is absent — agents arrive with no map of the codebase
roadmap.rationale: Without a CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md, any AI-assisted contribution starts from zero context on build/test commands (e.g. make static, the acceptance-tests harness), Jsonnet-specific domain nuance, and the implicit constraints maintainers already hold in their heads.
explore: What would a new contributor's first hour look like if the build/test/lint commands and an architecture map lived in a single agent-readable file?
Which of the constraints your maintainers hold implicitly (e.g. Jsonnet compatibility, kubectl/helm version pinning) would most reduce risk if written down for an agent to follow?

roadmap.title: The automation loop stops at dependency bumps — no AI review, fix, or ship loop exists yet
roadmap.rationale: Renovate reliably opens dependency PRs, but there's no AI review bot, no LLM-in-CI step, and no auto-fix loop; with only 3% of PRs showing any AI involvement, AI assistance today looks individual and ad hoc rather than embedded in the pipeline.
explore: Where in your current review cycle (median 1.3h to first review) would an AI review pass add signal before a human looks, versus just add noise?
Is there a category of routine PR — docs, chores, dependency follow-ups — where a bounded auto-fix-and-reopen loop feels safe to try first?

roadmap.title: There's no harness yet for verifying AI-authored changes before they reach human review
roadmap.rationale: Strong branch protection and signed commits mean the final gate is solid, but nothing upstream of that gate (evals, golden tests, an agents/ directory) currently gives confidence that an AI-proposed change to, say, the Jsonnet evaluation path behaves correctly before a human even opens the diff.
explore: If an agent proposed a change to core evaluation logic, what would 'tested and verified' look like before your reviewers spend time on it?
Would a small prompts/ or agents/ directory capturing recurring AI tasks (release notes, dependency triage, doc updates) make that work repeatable rather than one-off?

roadmap.title: Most CI workflows run with default, unscoped token permissions
roadmap.rationale: Signed commits and pinned actions are already in place, but only 2 of 7 workflows declare an explicit least-privilege `permissions:` block (one grants broad write) — a gap that matters more once any auto-merge or agentic step is introduced, since its blast radius would inherit whatever the workflow already has.
explore: For the workflows that don't yet declare `permissions:`, what's the minimum each one actually needs to do its job?
Would tightening this now make it easier to trust an autonomous PR or fix bot later, since its potential blast radius would already be bounded?

roadmap.title: Acceptance tests confirm the CLI runs, but many assertions stop at 'no error' rather than checking output
roadmap.rationale: The end-to-end acceptance suite is a real asset, but several cases lean on require.NoError alone rather than asserting on the resulting output — a regression that silently changes behavior (rather than crashing) could slip through, which becomes a sharper risk once AI-authored changes start landing in the same code paths.
explore: For the acceptance tests that only check 'no error', what would you want asserted if you were reviewing an AI-written patch to that same command?
Is there a Jsonnet-evaluation edge case where a golden-file or snapshot comparison would catch more than today's checks do?

discrepancies.claim: The signal reports 'sampled tests assert nothing' / '0 substantive assertions', but the sampled acceptance-tests files clearly use testify's require.Equal (comparing round-tripped Kubernetes ConfigMap objects in show_test.go), require.Contains (checking CLI help/output content in flag_test.go and help_test.go), and assert.FileExists/NoFileExists (verifying selective export behavior in export_test.go) — these are substantive behavioral assertions, not mere file-presence counting.
